title: Chromosomes, DNA and chromosome sets — video support
purpose: Distinguish chromatin, chromosomes, homologous chromosomes and chromosome sets.
fallback: A typical human body cell has 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs. Most pairs are homologous: the two chromosomes have the same genes at corresponding positions. One typically comes from the mother and one from the father. The alleles, or versions of those genes, need not be identical. The sex chromosomes require care. In an XX pair the chromosomes are homologous; X and Y share some corresponding regions but are not matching copies over their whole lengths. Autosomes are the chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes. A karyotype arranges photographed chromosomes by size and other features. It helps examine chromosome number and larger structural differences; it does not directly reveal every DNA sequence or every possible genetic condition.

title: Mitosis: chromosome movement through the stages — video support
purpose: Trace prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, connecting visible events with accurate chromosome distribution.
fallback: During anaphase, sister chromatids separate. Each becomes an individual chromosome and moves toward its assigned pole. The important event is separation of the copies made during S phase. Mitosis does not normally pair maternal and paternal homologues into tetrads and separate those pairs as meiosis I does. A diploid cell uses mitosis to preserve the chromosome complement in the two daughter nuclei. If a diagram uses two colours for parental origin, each normal mitotic daughter receives both parental contributions. Do not place all maternal chromosomes in one daughter and all paternal chromosomes in the other.

title: Meiosis I and separation of homologous chromosomes — video support
purpose: Trace meiosis I and explain why separation of homologues produces haploid chromosome sets while chromatids remain paired.
fallback: At metaphase I, homologous pairs align at the equator. Their orientation relative to other pairs can vary. A replicated maternal homologue faces one pole and its paternal partner faces the other, but different pairs can orient independently. During anaphase I, the homologues separate. The sister chromatids of each chromosome normally remain joined. The event is therefore different from mitotic anaphase, which separates sister chromatids. After this distribution, each future daughter receives one chromosome of each homologous pair. It has one set rather than two. That is the reduction in ploidy.

title: Comparing mitosis and meiosis — video support
purpose: Compare replication, pairing, divisions, ploidy and genetic similarity in mitosis and meiosis.
fallback: Before both processes, DNA replication creates sister chromatids. In mitosis, chromosomes align individually and sister chromatids separate in one nuclear division. The result is normally two nuclei with matching chromosome complements. In meiosis I, homologues pair, may exchange segments and then separate. In meiosis II, the sister chromatids separate without another full replication. The result is usually four haploid nuclear products, with genetic differences arising from assortment and recombination. The presence of spindle fibres or condensed chromosomes alone does not distinguish the processes. Look for homologous pairing, which units separate and how chromosome sets change.

title: Nondisjunction and chromosome abnormalities — video support
purpose: Predict products of nondisjunction in meiosis I or II and distinguish aneuploidy from a change in whole chromosome sets.
fallback: If a homologous pair fails to separate in meiosis I and meiosis II otherwise proceeds normally, all four final products have an abnormal number for that chromosome type. Two have an extra chromosome, n + 1, and two are missing one, n − 1. If meiosis I is normal but sister chromatids fail to separate in one cell during meiosis II, two products can remain normal. The affected cell produces one n + 1 product and one n − 1 product. The other cell produces two normal n products. These predictions assume one specified error and otherwise normal divisions. Multiple errors can produce other patterns, so do not apply the simplified pattern without checking the question.

title: Sexual and asexual reproductive strategies — video support
purpose: Classify reproductive strategies from evidence, distinguish bacterial division from mitosis, and connect reproduction with genetic variation.
fallback: Asexual reproduction can establish offspring without finding a mate and can preserve a successful genotype. However, genetically similar descendants may share vulnerabilities when conditions change. Mutation can still create differences, so clones are not permanently immune to variation. Sexual reproduction can produce more varied allele combinations, potentially increasing the range of responses within offspring. It also involves costs such as gamete production and, in many organisms, finding or interacting with a mate. Neither strategy is universally best in every environment. Parthenogenesis involves development from an unfertilized egg. Because different organisms use different cellular mechanisms, read the supplied life-cycle information before assigning ploidy or claiming all resulting offspring are identical.

title: Life cycles and alternation of generations — video support
purpose: Trace mitosis, meiosis and fertilization through haploid and diploid stages, including sporophytes, spores and gametophytes.
fallback: A diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores through meiosis. A spore develops by mitosis into a haploid gametophyte. The gametophyte then produces haploid gametes by mitosis. When gametes fuse, the diploid zygote grows by mitosis into a new sporophyte. The surprising step for learners is gamete production by mitosis in the gametophyte. The parent stage is already haploid, so another reduction division is not needed. The meiotic products in this plant cycle are spores, not the final gametes. Spores and gametes therefore have different roles. A spore can grow into a multicellular stage without fusion. A gamete contributes to the next diploid stage through fertilization.
